correctness.rationale: PASS: Fourier normalization gives psi_2(t,x)=exp[-x²/(4(1+it))]/sqrt[2(1+it)]. For epsilon=2-alpha>0 the first-order variation of exp[-it|p|^alpha] is +it epsilon |p|² log|p|; the even Fourier transform has algebraic coefficient it sqrt(2pi) epsilon x^-3. The full proof controls the second-order difference uniformly at x comparable to sqrt(L), L=log(1/epsilon), using differentiation under the Gaussian integral, a near-zero dyadic partition and repeated integrations by parts; the remainder is lower than the leading wing by the necessary logarithmic factor. Defining y-3/2 log y=L+log[4(1+t²)^(5/4)/(sqrt(pi)t)]+s balances Gaussian modulus with the algebraic wing. The complex Gaussian phase gives theta=pi/2+atan(t)/2, and as y runs continuously to infinity the phase -ty covers infinitely many turns. Hence normalized intensity has the stated envelopes. An independent 40-digit cosine quadrature at t=.7,epsilon=10^-4 gave observed difference/Gaussian about -.65524-.94590i versus leading prediction -.66264-.74894i (absolute error .1971); separate logarithmic-Fourier derivative quadratures at x=14,17 gave respective leading-coefficient ratios 1.0633+.0503i and 1.0400+.0552i. These checks corroborate, not prove, uniform limits.
residual_risks: The uniform second-order remainder is the nonstandard analytic step; dyadic integration by parts requires maintaining integrability and uniformity as alpha approaches 2.
A finite epsilon value cannot establish the sharp limsup/liminf of continuously rotating phase.

value.rationale: PASS: Fractional dispersion produces a spatial algebraic wing that cannot be detected by taking alpha up to 2 at fixed x. Locating where it overtakes the classical Gaussian and giving an exact second-order logarithmic center and coherent interference envelopes answers a motivated noncommuting-limits question. The phase winding and sharp intensity oscillation are qualitative predictions beyond rederiving a stable-tail exponent.
residual_risks: Only the free linear model, fixed t>0 and a chosen Gaussian packet; no assertion about nonlinear waves, all times, or spatial dimensions beyond one.

limitations: A finite set of quadratures is not an analytic proof of the O(1/log epsilon) estimate or infinite oscillations.
No claim of novelty for standard Fourier-tail formulas, scalar stable-density exponents or nonlinear similarly named papers.
